headline: A solo developer built a local-first AI Operating System with 296,000 lines of code.
summary: A single developer has engineered a comprehensive AI operating system, comprising nearly 300,000 lines of code, emphasizing local-first processing and autonomy.
details: A developer has single-handedly created a local-first AI Operating System, a monumental task involving 296,000 lines of code. This project showcases an impressive feat of individual software engineering.

The "local-first" approach means the AI processes data directly on the user's device, enhancing privacy and enabling offline functionality. This design choice contrasts with cloud-dependent AI systems.

Building an entire operating system, especially one integrated with AI capabilities, typically requires a large team. This solo effort highlights the potential for dedicated individual developers to tackle complex projects.

The project was shared on the DEV platform, demonstrating a significant contribution to the open-source or independent development community. It offers a glimpse into future possibilities for personal AI computing.

headline_marked: [[Android may soon restrict On-Device ADB]] connections, impacting power users and developers
headline: Android may soon restrict On-Device ADB connections, impacting power users and developers
summary: A feature request on Google's IssueTracker suggests potential restrictions on On-Device ADB, citing security concerns and aiming to protect against 'bad actors'. This change could affect developers and power users relying on local ADB connections.
details: Google is reportedly considering restricting On-Device ADB connections, a move discussed in an ongoing feature request on its IssueTracker. This is not an official announcement but a proposal from a core ADB maintainer, citing security concerns.

ADB, or Android Debug Bridge, is a protocol developed by Google that grants developers high-level privileges and access to sensitive commands for testing Android devices and applications. It was originally designed for use over a USB connection between an Android device and a separate developer machine.

On-Device ADB refers to a niche use case where developers run an ADB client directly on their phone, typically via a terminal emulator like Termux. This client then connects to the local ADB daemon (ADBD) server using a loopback address (127.0.0.1) through ADB TCP/IP or Wireless Debugging.

The proposed restriction aims to protect against "bad actors" and aligns with Google's broader changes to sideloading. While enhancing security, this change could significantly impact power users and developers who rely on this local debugging method.

One notable impact would be on frameworks like Shizuku, which enable powerful applications without root access by leveraging On-Device ADB. Developers of such tools, including those creating accessibility solutions like call recorders for users with disabilities, would be affected.
